title: The Deobandi and Barelvi traditions
hookLine: two South Asian Sunni movements from the nineteenth century, differing on devotions to saints and the Prophet ﷺ

cards: Two mosques on the same street, in a city in Pakistan, or Bradford, or Chicago. Both Sunni. Both follow the Hanafi school of law.
Both pray the same prayers at the same times. At one, when Friday prayer ends, the whole room rises and sends greetings to the Prophet in Urdu poetry, together, standing.

At the other, people file out quietly, and a teacher stays behind for a class on following his Sunnah closely, which is how that teacher says he is best honored. Same street, same school. Different ways of showing honor.

teach.b: Both names come from places in north India. Deobandi is named for Deoband, a town where a religious school, the Darul Uloom, was founded by scholars including Muhammad Qasim Nanautawi and Rashid Ahmad Gangohi.
Barelvi is named for Bareilly, the hometown of the scholar Ahmad Raza Khan. Barelvi Muslims often prefer to call themselves Ahl al-Sunnah wa al-Jama'ah, the people of the Sunnah and the community.
What they share: both are Sunni, both Hanafi, both have Sufi teachers and lineages in their history, and both hold the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, at the center.

The Qur'an says, in Pickthall's translation: "Lo! Allah and His angels shower blessings on the Prophet. O ye who believe! Ask blessings on him and salute him with a worthy salutation." Neither disputes that.

Where they differ is how. Barelvi Muslims, in their own words, express love for the Prophet openly: the Mawlid, his birthday, with gatherings, poetry and standing to greet him, and honoring the saints at their shrines.
Ahmad Raza Khan himself wrote devotional poetry in the Prophet's praise.

Deobandi Muslims, in their own words, put the weight on following the Sunnah closely, are cautious about practices they see as later additions, including some of these, and built a network of madrasas focused on study.
The disagreements are real, and sometimes sharp.

teach.h: HOLD FAST, ALL OF YOU TOGETHER.
teach.b: But the two mosques share a school, a creed and a Prophet, and one line of the Qur'an hangs over both doors: "And hold fast, all of you together, to the cable of Allah, and do not separate."

how: Deobandi and Barelvi Muslims are Sunni Muslims of the Hanafi school with roots in South Asia and communities around the world; Barelvi communities often celebrate the Mawlid and honor saints' shrines, while Deobandi communities emphasize close following of the Sunnah and madrasa study and are cautious about some of those practices.

games.why: Barelvi communities often celebrate the Mawlid with gatherings and poetry; Deobandi communities put the weight on following the Sunnah closely, and are cautious about some of those practices.

practice: Bring back the two mosques: the room rising with poetry sung together, then the quiet class and the close reading. Notice that both are trying to honor the same person.
If you pray, send blessings on the Prophet, as the verse asks; if not, simply hold both rooms in mind together.
